techniques.description: Developing your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — the strongest course of action you'll take if this negotiation fails. A strong BATNA is your source of power. You never negotiate without knowing exactly what you'll do if you walk away.
techniques.practice_prompt: You're negotiating a job offer. Before you discuss salary, articulate your BATNA aloud: 'If this doesn't work out, my best alternative is [specific option]. I have [competing offer / current job / freelance pipeline]. My walk-away number is [X] because below that, my alternative is better.' Be specific — a vague BATNA is no BATNA at all.
success_criteria: BATNA is specific and concrete, not vague ('I'll figure something out')
Can articulate exactly what they'll do if this negotiation fails
Tone conveys genuine confidence in the alternative — they'd actually take it
Derives a clear reservation point (walk-away number) from the BATNA
Distinguishes between BATNA (best alternative) and wishful thinking
common_mistakes: BATNA is too vague ('I'll find something else')
Confusing a weak BATNA with no BATNA (everyone has one — it might just be bad)
Overestimating their BATNA (wishful thinking disguised as preparation)
Not connecting BATNA to a concrete walk-away threshold
Tone that reveals their BATNA is actually weak despite confident words
techniques.structure: State the negotiation context (10s) → articulate the BATNA specifically (15s) → derive the walk-away number/threshold (15s) → state commitment to the threshold with conviction (15s)
techniques.coaching_notes: BATNA is the single most important concept in negotiation theory. It's also where voice analysis adds the most value — users who SAY they're comfortable walking away but whose voice reveals stress are overestimating their BATNA. The gap between stated confidence and vocal markers is the diagnostic signal.

techniques.description: Saying no without damaging the relationship, using Ury's Yes-No-Yes structure: Yes to yourself (affirm what matters to you), No to the request (clear boundary), Yes to the relationship (offer an alternative or express continued respect). The structure: 'Because I value X [yes], I can't do Y [no]. What I can do is Z [yes].'
techniques.practice_prompt: Your boss asks you to take on a third project when you're already at capacity. Practice the positive no: 'I care about delivering quality on the Henderson and Rivera accounts — that's my commitment to you [Yes to self]. I can't take on the Morrison project without one of those suffering [No to request]. What I can do is help you find the right person for Morrison, or take it on in March when Henderson wraps [Yes to relationship].'
success_criteria: Follows the Yes-No-Yes structure clearly
First 'yes' affirms a genuine value or commitment
The 'no' is clear and direct — not hedged or apologetic
Second 'yes' offers a concrete alternative or preserves the relationship
Tone is respectful and firm, not defensive or aggressive
common_mistakes: Skipping the first 'yes' — jumping straight to no without anchoring in values
Making the 'no' too soft ('I'm not sure I can...' instead of 'I can't')
Forgetting the second 'yes' — leaving the other person with just a rejection
Tone that undermines the no (apologetic, pleading, or angry)
Offering an alternative that's actually the same thing repackaged
techniques.structure: Yes to yourself — state what matters (15s) → No to the request — clear and direct (10s) → Yes to the relationship — offer alternative (20s) → reflection on the structure (10s)
techniques.coaching_notes: The Positive No is Ury's most practically useful technique for everyday life. It works in negotiations, workplace conversations, and personal relationships. Voice analysis focus: is the 'no' firm (steady pitch, measured pace) or weakened (rising pitch, rushed delivery)? The quality of the 'no' determines whether it sticks.

techniques.description: Treating the other person as a partner tackling a shared problem rather than an adversary to defeat. Attacks the problem, not the person. When emotions rise, redirect energy from 'you vs. me' to 'us vs. the problem.'
techniques.practice_prompt: Your business partner blames you for a failed product launch: 'If you'd listened to me about the timeline, we wouldn't be in this mess.' Instead of defending yourself, separate the person from the problem: 'We're both frustrated with how the launch went — and we both want the next one to succeed. Instead of debating what went wrong, can we spend this time designing a launch process that addresses the timeline issues?'
success_criteria: Redirects from blame/attack to shared problem-solving
Uses 'we' language rather than 'you' or 'I'
Acknowledges the emotion without getting pulled into it
Proposes a concrete shift to working on the problem together
Tone is warm and forward-looking, not dismissive of their feelings
common_mistakes: Sounding dismissive of their concerns ('Let's just move on')
Defending themselves before separating the person from the problem
Using 'we' language but still attacking ('We both know you caused this')
Being so focused on de-escalation that they don't acknowledge the real issue
Forcing the shift too quickly — the other person needs to feel heard first
techniques.structure: Hear the attack/blame (5s) → acknowledge the shared frustration (10s) → reframe as a shared problem (20s) → propose collaborative next step (15s) → check for buy-in (5s)
techniques.coaching_notes: This is the most fundamental Ury principle and the easiest to learn but hardest to execute under pressure. Voice analysis should measure: does the user's vocal stress decrease when they shift to problem-mode, or does residual defensiveness leak through? The shift from adversarial to collaborative has a measurable vocal signature — lower pitch, slower pace, fewer filler words.

techniques.description: Expanding the negotiation pie before dividing it. Instead of fighting over a fixed set of resources, generate creative options that create value for both sides. Requires separating inventing from deciding — brainstorm first, evaluate later.
techniques.practice_prompt: You and a co-worker both want the corner office. Instead of arguing about who deserves it, invent options: 'What if we thought bigger than the office? What do we each actually need? I need quiet for focus work. You need space for client meetings. What if we redesigned the office layout so we both get what we actually need, even if neither of us gets the corner?' Generate 3 creative alternatives.
success_criteria: Generates at least 3 distinct options beyond the obvious two positions
Options create new value rather than just splitting the existing value
Identifies underlying interests rather than surface positions
Tone is genuinely creative and exploratory — brainstorming energy
Separates the inventing phase from the judging phase
common_mistakes: Generating options that only serve their own interests
Evaluating options while still brainstorming (kills creativity)
Only generating variations of splitting the difference (not truly creative)
Not probing deep enough for underlying interests behind positions
Proposing options as if presenting a final deal rather than brainstorming
techniques.structure: Identify the surface conflict (10s) → probe for underlying interests (15s) → brainstorm 3 creative options aloud (25s) → identify the most promising option (10s)
techniques.coaching_notes: This is the most creative technique in the entire collection. It requires genuine lateral thinking under pressure. Voice analysis value: creative brainstorming has a distinct vocal pattern — variable pitch, exploratory pace, rising inflection. If the user sounds flat or monotone during brainstorming, they're not truly in creative mode. Coach them to think aloud with genuine curiosity.
